articles.title: Rochdale Man Sentenced to Six Years for Violent and Sexual Offences
articles.excerpt: A man has been sentenced to six years in prison following a series of violent and sexual offences against a 16-year-old survivor, thanks to an investigation by Operation Soteria.
articles.content_html:
A man has been sentenced to six years in prison following a series of violent and sexual offences against a 16-year-old survivor. The sentencing took place as a result of an investigation by Operation Soteria.

The survivor's bravery in coming forward played a crucial role in the case, allowing the authorities to take action against the perpetrator. The investigation highlighted the importance of supporting victims of such crimes.

The court heard details of the offences, which took place over a period of time, causing significant distress to the victim. The judge acknowledged the impact of the crimes on the survivor's life.

This case underscores the ongoing efforts by law enforcement to tackle violent and sexual offences and to provide justice for victims. Anyone with information can find Greater Manchester Police and Crimestoppers contact details at the end of this article.

articles.title: Editorial: Justice remains unfinished in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: More than a decade after the Rochdale grooming gang scandal shocked Britain, the perpetrators have been jailed, reforms have been introduced and institutions have apologised. Yet for many survivors and residents, questions about accountability, trust and whether justice has truly been delivered remain unanswered.
articles.content_html:
More than a decade has passed since the Rochdale child sexual exploitation scandal exposed one of the gravest safeguarding failures in modern British history. The men responsible have been convicted and imprisoned, but the question that continues to confront Rochdale is whether justice ended with those convictions.

Successive independent inquiries have reached strikingly similar conclusions. Reviews by Parliament, local safeguarding bodies and independent investigators found that vulnerable children were repeatedly failed by institutions responsible for protecting them. Victims were too often viewed as making 'lifestyle choices' rather than recognised as children subjected to coercion, rape, trafficking and organised sexual exploitation. Information was not consistently shared between agencies, warning signs were missed, organised offending was underestimated and opportunities to intervene were repeatedly lost.

The testimony of survivors remains among the most compelling evidence of those failures. Girls described repeatedly reporting abuse only to be disbelieved, dismissed as troublesome teenagers or treated as willing participants in their own exploitation. Children who regularly went missing were returned to the same environments where offenders continued to target them. Independent reviews concluded that professionals frequently focused on victims' behaviour rather than the methods of coercion used by organised offenders.

The criminal justice system eventually delivered significant convictions. Operation Span resulted in nine men being convicted in 2012 for offences including rape, trafficking and conspiracy to engage in sexual activity with children. Further investigations have led to additional prosecutions linked to historic child sexual exploitation across Greater Manchester. Judges described the offending as calculated, organised and profoundly damaging, recognising that many victims would carry lifelong psychological trauma.

Yet convictions answered only one question: the guilt of the offenders. They did not answer why children were repeatedly failed before those prosecutions ever reached a courtroom.

The official inquiries found that the primary problem was not an absence of legislation. The criminal offences already existed. Rather, agencies failed to recognise organised grooming, safeguarding procedures were inconsistently applied, intelligence was not always effectively shared and vulnerable children were too often judged instead of protected. Some reviews also concluded that concerns about community tensions influenced professional decision-making in certain cases, although they stressed that institutional failures were complex and involved multiple contributing factors.

Political debate over those failures continues today. Sir Keir Starmer has consistently defended his record as Director of Public Prosecutions, pointing to reforms introduced after the Rochdale prosecutions that encouraged prosecutors to focus more closely on suspect behaviour rather than relying heavily on assessments of victim credibility. Nigel Farage has repeatedly argued that institutional accountability remains incomplete and has called for wider national inquiries into organised child sexual exploitation.

Independent MP Rupert Lowe commissioned his own inquiry into grooming gangs, arguing that previous investigations had failed to provide full transparency or accountability. Lowe's report calls for mandatory recording of offender ethnicity, stronger criminal justice responses, improved national data collection and further investigation into institutional failings. While his inquiry does not carry statutory authority, it has become part of the continuing national debate surrounding organised child sexual exploitation and institutional responsibility.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan also faced criticism after asking for clarification during a London Assembly meeting about what was meant by the phrase 'grooming gangs' before responding more broadly on child sexual exploitation. The exchange became part of the wider political discussion over how public authorities describe organised abuse and communicate with victims and the public.

There have unquestionably been improvements since the original scandal. Greater Manchester Police has established dedicated child sexual exploitation capabilities, multi-agency safeguarding arrangements have been strengthened, inspection reports have recognised improvements in identifying vulnerable children and historic offenders continue to face prosecution years after their crimes. Those reforms are significant and should not be dismissed.

However, reform is not the same as accountability.

For many survivors, organisational apologies and revised procedures have never fully addressed the institutional failures identified by successive inquiries. Former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver has repeatedly argued that child sexual exploitation remains a continuing threat and has warned against believing the lessons of Rochdale have been fully learned. She has consistently maintained that safeguarding depends not only on procedures but on professionals who are prepared to challenge assumptions, recognise organised exploitation and place children's welfare above institutional reputation.

Child sexual exploitation has not disappeared. Police forces across England and Wales continue to investigate organised grooming offences while offenders increasingly exploit social media, encrypted messaging platforms, online coercion and county lines criminality. Organised abuse evolves. Safeguarding must evolve with it.

The greatest lesson from Rochdale is not that Britain lacked the legal powers to prosecute offenders. It is that institutions repeatedly failed to use those powers when vulnerable children first asked for help. Children who should have been believed were doubted. Warning signs that should have triggered intervention were overlooked. Opportunities to prevent further abuse were lost.

Rochdale Borough Council has acknowledged profound institutional failings and apologised to survivors. Public bodies have accepted that serious mistakes were made, while successive reforms have sought to strengthen safeguarding and improve inter-agency cooperation. Those changes deserve recognition.

Whether they have fully restored public trust is another question entirely.

Justice cannot be measured solely by the length of prison sentences imposed on offenders. It is also measured by whether institutions learn from catastrophic failure, whether public officials accept responsibility when safeguarding collapses and whether every vulnerable child reporting abuse today can expect to be believed, protected and acted upon without hesitation.

Until survivors believe those standards have been achieved, and until the public is confident that institutional accountability carries meaningful consequences as well as organisational reform, many will continue to conclude that justice in Rochdale remains unfinished.

articles.title: Kirkholt and the fight against knife crime: why prevention matters as much as policing
articles.excerpt: Knife crime remains a concern for many families in Kirkholt, but police, youth workers and community groups say prevention, education and opportunity are just as important as enforcement in keeping young people safe.
articles.content_html:
Knife crime remains one of the issues that concerns many families across Kirkholt and the wider Rochdale borough. While high-profile incidents often make headlines, community leaders, police and youth organisations all agree that preventing young people from carrying knives in the first place is just as important as enforcing the law against those who do.

Although Rochdale has lower levels of knife crime than several other parts of Greater Manchester, it continues to experience incidents involving bladed weapons, particularly in areas facing higher levels of deprivation. The borough's Strategic Threat Assessment notes that knife crime is more common in town centres and some residential neighbourhoods where poverty is greatest, while young people are disproportionately affected as both victims and offenders. It also found that some children told youth workers they carried knives because they believed it offered protection or improved their image among peers.

For communities such as Kirkholt, the challenge is not simply about policing but understanding why some young people feel the need to carry a weapon. Youth workers and charities frequently point to a combination of social pressures, fear of becoming a victim, exploitation by organised criminals, school exclusion, adverse childhood experiences and limited opportunities as factors that can increase vulnerability.

Greater Manchester Police has continued to target violent crime through proactive neighbourhood policing, stop-and-search powers where legally justified and intelligence-led operations against drug dealing and organised crime. Officers covering Balderstone and Kirkholt currently identify drug dealing, off-road bikes and wider neighbourhood crime as local priorities, with regular patrols aimed at disrupting criminal activity and reassuring residents.

There have also been encouraging signs across the borough. Greater Manchester Police says knife crime in Rochdale reduced during the second half of 2024 compared with the first six months of the year, while more than 100 knives were surrendered through permanent amnesty bins installed at local police stations. Officers say removing weapons from circulation is one part of a broader strategy to reduce serious violence.

Community organisations argue, however, that enforcement alone cannot solve the problem. Providing safe places for young people to spend time, investing in youth services, sports clubs and mentoring programmes, and creating better employment opportunities are all seen as essential to reducing the long-term appeal of gangs and weapon carrying.

Parents also have an important role. Talking openly about peer pressure, recognising changes in behaviour and encouraging children to seek help if they feel threatened can all help prevent situations from escalating. Schools across Greater Manchester continue to work alongside police and youth services to educate pupils about the devastating consequences of carrying knives, not only for victims but for those who choose to carry them.

For most people living in Kirkholt, knife crime is not something they encounter in everyday life. The vast majority of residents simply want safe streets, strong communities and opportunities for young people to succeed. Nevertheless, every incident involving a knife has the potential to leave lasting consequences for families and neighbourhoods.

Reducing knife crime ultimately depends on a combination of effective policing, early intervention and community support. While officers continue to target those involved in serious violence, many local organisations believe the greatest success will come from ensuring fewer young people ever feel the need to pick up a knife in the first place.

articles.title: Rochdale TikToker Under Police Investigation for Secret Filming
articles.excerpt: Scott Margerison, known as "E Dobbin," is under investigation after allegedly using smart glasses to film the public during a road trip in Scotland.
articles.content_html:
A TikToker from Rochdale named Scott Margerison, known online as "E Dobbin," is under police investigation following allegations of secretly filming members of the public during a road trip across Scotland in late June and early July.

Margerison reportedly used Meta smart glasses to record footage without the consent of those being filmed. The investigation has raised concerns regarding privacy and consent in public spaces.

Police are looking into the circumstances surrounding the filming and whether any laws were breached during the recordings. No further details about the investigation have been released.

Anyone with information can find Greater Manchester Police and Crimestoppers contact details at the end of this article.

articles.title: Rochdale-born TikToker investigated by Scottish police over Meta smart glasses videos
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale-born TikTok creator known online as 'E Dobbin' is being investigated by Scottish police after complaints relating to videos recorded using Meta smart glasses.
articles.content_html:
Scott Margerison, a Rochdale native who publishes content online under the alias 'E Dobbin', is being investigated by Scottish police following complaints about videos allegedly recorded using Meta smart glasses during a trip around Scotland.

According to the Daily Record, officers are reviewing footage to determine whether any criminal offences have been committed. The reported videos include members of the public, retail staff and CalMac employees being recorded, along with confrontational interactions and footage from the bridge of the CalMac ferry Loch Seaforth. CalMac subsequently suspended public bridge visits.

Previous controversies

The Scotland investigation is not the first controversy surrounding Margerison's online activity. He previously attracted significant public criticism after uploading footage filmed inside JD Gym in which viewers alleged he made racist and sexually explicit remarks while recording members of the public. Reports at the time indicated he was subsequently banned from the gym.

Online content

Across multiple TikTok accounts, some of which are no longer available, Margerison has published videos promoting numerous conspiracy theories and alternative historical claims. These include the Tartaria conspiracy theory, claims that the Apollo Moon landings were faked, the so-called Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory, and claims that mountains are the fossilised remains of enormous petrified creatures.

The Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory has been widely rejected by historians and researchers and is commonly associated with antisemitic conspiracy narratives.

Many of Margerison's videos challenge established historical, archaeological and scientific consensus and have generated substantial debate and criticism online.

Police investigation

Scottish police have confirmed officers received complaints and are reviewing the available material to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.

At the time of publication no criminal charges have been announced. An investigation does not imply criminal guilt.

articles.title: Investigation Launched Following Fire at Illegal Waste Site in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The Environment Agency has confirmed an investigation into a fire at an illegal waste site in Rochdale, which required extensive firefighting efforts.
articles.content_html:
An investigation has been launched following a fire at a waste site in Rochdale. Crews worked throughout the night on July 24 after a fire broke out off Spring Mill Walk, in Smallbridge. Firefighters were called to the scene at 8.15pm and worked until around 1pm the following day.

Thick plumes of smoke were visible for miles around as six fire engines and specialist equipment were deployed to extinguish the fire. The Environment Agency became involved due to the large quantity of waste at the site.

In an update issued on August 1, the Environment Agency confirmed that the fire occurred at an illegal waste site, which is now under investigation. Residents in the surrounding area were advised to keep their windows and doors closed during the incident.

The scale of the operation faced by firefighters was significant, with dramatic images showing the extent of the fire. The investigation will seek to determine the cause and circumstances surrounding the incident.

articles.content_html:

The appeal follows concerns about Blake's compliance with the terms of his release. Police are keen to locate him as soon as possible to ensure public safety.

articles.title: Man jailed for taking weapons to Heywood school
articles.excerpt: A man has been sentenced to two years in prison after taking a hammer, hatchet and kitchen knife to a school in Heywood, intending to create a scene for attention regarding his asylum status.
articles.content_html:
A man has been sentenced to two years in prison after taking a hammer, a hatchet and a kitchen knife to a school in Heywood. Both Douk Deng, 21, a South Sudanese national, was jailed after he was found on the premises of Edgar Wood Academy on August 6 last year.

Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court heard that Deng had become increasingly frustrated with immigration authorities for not providing assistance in his attempts to remain in the UK. He had applied for asylum three times, all of which were refused. Deng intended to 'create a scene for attention' to aid his cause, the court was told.

Deng was arrested after workmen confronted him at the school. Prior to this, a member of the public had alerted the authorities after seeing him behaving oddly in the street nearby, carrying a petrol can with a hammer tied to his belt. He was observed walking around the school, which was closed to pupils for the summer, mumbling to himself before builders on site called the police.

The incident raised concerns about safety at the school, although no injuries were reported. Deng's actions have highlighted ongoing issues surrounding the treatment of asylum seekers in the UK.

articles.title: Two Drug Dealers Sentenced for Running Rochdale's 'Adam Line'
articles.excerpt: Two men have been sentenced for their roles in a Rochdale drug operation known as the 'Adam Line', which has been linked to significant criminal activity in the area.
articles.content_html:
Two drug dealers have been sentenced for their involvement in a notorious Rochdale drugs line known as the 'Adam Line', which has persisted despite multiple police operations aimed at dismantling it. Haider Ali, 34, known as 'The Ghost', and Alan Ronald Ohara, 47, referred to as 'Rocket Ronny', were arrested last year while operating the line, which is believed to generate at least £1 million annually.

During a police operation, officers observed what appeared to be a drug deal taking place on Baron Street in Rochdale. Following a Nissan Qashqai, they apprehended Ali, who attempted to flee but was caught nearby. He was found in possession of £1,000 in cash, along with wraps of cocaine and heroin. Police discovered additional drugs in the vehicle, including 75 wraps of cocaine and 32 wraps of heroin. Prosecutors described Ali as the 'controller' of the Adam drugs line.

Ohara, who was driving the car, was also arrested, along with a 17-year-old boy named Shane Walsh, who was acting as Ali's 'trusted lieutenant'. Walsh was responsible for preparing drugs for sale. Evidence from mobile phones seized during the arrests indicated that the trio was heavily involved in the drug operation, with Walsh's phone containing lists of debts and expenses related to his drug dealing activities. Despite being released on bail, Walsh continued to engage in drug dealing until his second arrest.

The court heard that Walsh had been a victim of grooming and exploitation, having moved to Rochdale from Middleton due to personal issues. His involvement in the drug culture began at a young age, and he had been linked to the operation since he was 16. Ohara's messages revealed he was more than just a driver, discussing plans to establish his own drugs line. The case highlights ongoing challenges in tackling drug-related crime in Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale Police Launch Knife Amnesty Scheme
articles.excerpt: Rochdale police have introduced a knife amnesty scheme, allowing residents to anonymously dispose of knives and bladed weapons at designated bins across the district.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale police have launched a "Forever Amnesty" scheme, enabling residents to safely and anonymously dispose of knives and bladed weapons. The initiative features 13 permanent amnesty bins located across ten local districts, with three bins specifically situated in the Rochdale district.

The scheme aims to reduce knife crime and promote community safety by providing a secure method for individuals to surrender dangerous items without fear of prosecution.

Residents can find the amnesty bins at various locations throughout Rochdale, encouraging participation from the community to help create a safer environment.

This initiative is part of a broader effort by local authorities to address concerns surrounding knife crime and to foster a culture of safety within the community.
